On the human side, the affected group is the up to 35–50 scientific and support personnel at the field camp, plus other nations' Antarctic operating organizations across the broader continent, where fewer than 50 isolated stations occupy 5.5 million square miles. summary.alternatives_overview.extracted_value: NSF concludes that the scientific goals cannot be achieved without occupying the drill site, so a no-project alternative is not recommended. An alternative of hauling all liquid and solid wastes back to McMurdo Station, instead of on-site burning, burial, and subsurface sewage disposal into the firn, was considered but rejected as neither environmentally necessary nor economically feasible. To address the small chance of hitting an oil deposit, two alternatives were weighed and rejected: running a seismic survey from below the shelf after breakthrough to map sediment structures (specialists said the data would be of limited value unless a much larger program were mounted), and simply not drilling into the sediment and bedrock (rejected because the planned hydrocarbon monitoring and safety measures are considered adequate). Reviewer-suggested alternatives discussed in the comments include conducting a seismic refraction survey before drilling rather than 'drilling blindly,' incinerating sanitary wastes instead of firn discharge, avoiding diesel oil as drilling fluid unless it can be recaptured, and plugging and abandoning the hole (or shifting to another drill site) if substantial hydrocarbons are encountered.
summary.alternatives_overview.evidence_quote: The remote possibility of penetrating an oil deposit suggests two alternatives
summary.alternatives_overview.note: The value accurately summarizes Part IV (page 5) alternatives (no-project, waste hauling to McMurdo, seismic survey post-breakthrough, no sediment drilling) and reviewer-suggested alternatives from pages 70, 76, 78. Dismissal rationales are given on page 5 and in the responses on pages 68 and 76.

summary.environmental_impact.extracted_value: NSF concludes that no impacts of great magnitude are expected and that effects will be short-term and highly localized around the camp and drill site. Routine impacts include compaction of snow and firn under the LC-130 ski airstrip and toboggan trails, minor local air emissions from aircraft and generators, incineration of combustible trash, and noise and vibration from generators and drilling. Sanitary wastewater will be discharged below the surface into the permeable firn, forming a subsurface pool roughly 60 m across that will freeze back within about a year and eventually reach the ice front in about 1,000 years as the shelf moves seaward. Non-combustible solid wastes such as batteries, plastics, and rubber will be back-hauled to McMurdo and shipped to the U.S. Navy salvage yard at Port Hueneme, California, while liquid radioisotope wastes will be stored in metal containers for return. The most serious — but explicitly 'remote' — risk is drilling into a pressurized oil deposit in the sea-floor sediments: drilling to 100 m is considered safe, 150 m marginal, cores will be continuously inspected using gas chromatography for hydrocarbons from methane through hexane, and cement and bentonite will be on hand to plug the hole; a spill under 300–500 m of ice would be essentially impossible to clean up, and released oil could eventually reach the Ross Sea and affect penguins, seabirds, seals, and any biota beneath the shelf.

summary.overview.extracted_value: The Ross Ice Shelf Project (RISP) is a National Science Foundation research effort, run by the University of Nebraska, to drill through the roughly 500-meter-thick Ross Ice Shelf in Antarctica and sample the ice, the ~200-meter water column beneath it, and the sea-floor sediments below. The site is uninhabited by people; the affected environment is the ice shelf itself, the water and sea-floor beneath it, any specialized biota under the shelf, and — in the event of an oil release — penguins, seabirds, and seals of the Ross Sea. NSF considered but rejected a no-project alternative and back-hauling all wastes to McMurdo, and weighed reviewer suggestions such as running a seismic survey before drilling, incinerating sanitary wastes, and plugging or relocating the hole if hydrocarbons appear. Expected impacts are described as short-term and highly localized — snow compaction from ski-equipped aircraft, minor air emissions, noise, subsurface disposal of sanitary wastewater into the firn, and buried or back-hauled solid waste — with the main serious risk being a remote chance of drilling into a pressurized oil deposit, which under 300–500 m of ice would be essentially impossible to clean up. Five federal agencies commented on the draft; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) rated it 'ER' (Environmental Reservations) and Category 2 (Insufficient Information), the State Department said it 'glosses over' oil-spill impacts, and NSF responded with details on a prior seismic survey, gas-chromatograph core monitoring, and plans to plug the hole if substantial hydrocarbons are found.
summary.overview.evidence_quote: we have classified the project as ER (Environmental Reservations) and rated the draft statement as Category 2 (Insufficient Information)
summary.overview.note: All claims verified against cited pages. Key figures (500-m ice thickness, 200-m water depth, 300–500 m cleanup impossibility) match exactly. EPA rating, State Department quote, and agency count all confirmed verbatim. Acronyms NSF, EPA, and RISP are all expanded on first use within the value.

summary.project_description.extracted_value: The Ross Ice Shelf Project (RISP) is a multi-year National Science Foundation research operation, carried out by the University of Nebraska, to drill several holes through the roughly 500-meter-thick Ross Ice Shelf at about 82°22'S, 168°40'W, in order to sample the ice, the ~200-meter water column below it, and the sea-floor sediments and bedrock. The drilling program includes a ~100-m water well, a 16.5-cm-diameter cored hole through the shelf, a 30-cm gas-extraction hole, and a 30-cm access hole kept open by an electric heating cable so instruments and sampling gear can be lowered through it. The site was chosen to be crevasse-free and located about 300+ km from the seaward edge of the shelf; core samples will be analyzed for physical, chemical, gas, isotopic, and biological properties. The work is supported by a field camp of Jamesway huts for up to 35–50 people over roughly four to five months, supplied by ski-equipped LC-130 and Twin Otter aircraft from McMurdo Station.

summary.public_response.extracted_value: The final Environmental Impact Statement (EIS) was made available to the Council on Environmental Quality and the public on June 30, 1976. Written comments on the draft came from five federal agencies — the Departments of Transportation, Interior, and State, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the U.S. Atomic Energy Commission — with no public or non-governmental commenters described. The Coast Guard (for U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT)) and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) pressed for a pre-drilling seismic survey and more detail on hydrocarbon-release precautions; the State Department said the draft 'glosses over' the potential impact of an oil spill; EPA rated the draft 'ER' (Environmental Reservations) and Category 2 (Insufficient Information), asked for a glossary of technical terms, and suggested analyzing cores for radionuclides such as uranium, thorium, and radium; Interior and AEC largely concurred, with AEC agreeing the impact would be 'largely negligible' relative to the scientific benefits. NSF responded that a 1974–75 seismic refraction study on the Ross Ice Shelf had already found sediments up to 2 km thick (averaging about 1.5 km), that cores would be gas-chromatograph monitored, and that the hole would be plugged if substantial hydrocarbons appeared.
summary.public_response.evidence_quote: Our review of the Statement does indicate that the impact of performing the RISP appears to have been largely anticipated by NSF, and we agree with the conclusion that the impact will be largely negligible as opposed to the scientific benefits derived from RISP.
summary.public_response.note: All claims verified against cited pages. DOT/Coast Guard seismic survey recommendation (p.70), State Dept 'glosses over' quote (p.75), EPA ER/Category 2 rating and glossary/radionuclide suggestions (pp.77-79), NSF reply on 2km/1.5km avg sediments and chromatograph monitoring (p.80), AEC 'largely negligible' concurrence (p.84), availability date June 30, 1976 (p.6).
